questions.stem: In a linear programming problem, what is the objective function?
options: The quantity to be maximised or minimised
The inequality that limits each resource
The region where all constraints are met
The corner point where two lines meet
questions.explanation: The objective function, such as profit P = 5x + 4y, is what is being optimised. The inequalities are the constraints, and the region satisfying them all is the feasible region.

questions.stem: In linear programming, what is the feasible region?
options: The point that gives the largest objective value
The area beneath the graph of the objective function
The set of points that satisfy every constraint
The set of points that satisfy at least one constraint
questions.explanation: A point is feasible only if it obeys all the constraints at once, so the feasible region is where all the shaded half-planes overlap. The optimal point is one particular point inside or on the edge of it.

questions.stem: Where is the optimal solution of a linear programming problem with a bounded feasible region found?
options: At the centre of the feasible region
Wherever the region crosses the x-axis
Wherever the region crosses the y-axis
At a vertex of the feasible region
questions.explanation: As a line of constant profit slides across the region, the last point it touches is a corner. So the objective function is evaluated at each vertex and the best value chosen. Points on an axis are only optimal if they happen to be vertices.

questions.stem: Students make x koalas and y wombats from leftover materials. A koala uses 1 m of fabric and 3 kg of stuffing; a wombat uses 2 m of fabric and 2 kg of stuffing. They have 40 m of fabric and 60 kg of stuffing. Which inequality represents the fabric constraint?
questions.explanation: Each koala uses 1 m and each wombat 2 m, so the fabric used is x + 2y, which cannot exceed the 40 m available. Using ≥ would force at least 40 m to be used.

questions.stem: Students make x koalas and y wombats from leftover materials. A koala uses 1 m of fabric and 3 kg of stuffing; a wombat uses 2 m of fabric and 2 kg of stuffing. They have 40 m of fabric and 60 kg of stuffing. Which inequality represents the stuffing constraint?
questions.explanation: Koalas use 3 kg each and wombats 2 kg each, so stuffing used is 3x + 2y, at most 60 kg. Swapping the coefficients matches the amounts to the wrong toy.

questions.stem: Why do most linear programming problems include the constraints x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0?
options: The vertices must all have whole-number values
The quantities made or used cannot be negative
The objective function must always be positive
The feasible region must contain the origin
questions.explanation: x and y count things such as toys or kilograms, so negative values have no meaning. These non-negativity constraints keep the feasible region in the first quadrant.

questions.stem: When graphing x + 2y ≤ 40, the test point (0, 0) is substituted. What does the result show?
options: 0 ≤ 40 is true, so the side without (0, 0) is feasible
0 ≤ 40 is false, so the side containing (0, 0) is feasible
The test shows only where the boundary line crosses an axis
0 ≤ 40 is true, so the side containing (0, 0) is feasible
questions.explanation: Substituting (0, 0) gives 0 ≤ 40, which is true, so every point on the same side of the line as the origin satisfies the constraint. If the test were false, the other side would be shaded.

questions.stem: Students make x koalas and y wombats from leftover materials. A koala uses 1 m of fabric and 3 kg of stuffing; a wombat uses 2 m of fabric and 2 kg of stuffing. They have 40 m of fabric and 60 kg of stuffing. The constraints are x + 2y ≤ 40, 3x + 2y ≤ 60, x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0. At which vertex do the fabric and stuffing lines intersect?
questions.explanation: Subtracting x + 2y = 40 from 3x + 2y = 60 gives 2x = 20, so x = 10 and y = (40 − 10)/2 = 15. (15, 10) swaps the coordinates and uses only 35 m of fabric, so it is not on the fabric line.

questions.stem: Students make x koalas and y wombats from leftover materials. A koala uses 1 m of fabric and 3 kg of stuffing; a wombat uses 2 m of fabric and 2 kg of stuffing. They have 40 m of fabric and 60 kg of stuffing. The constraints are x + 2y ≤ 40, 3x + 2y ≤ 60, x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0. Besides (0, 0), what are the vertices of the feasible region on the axes?
questions.explanation: On the x-axis the stuffing constraint binds first: 3x ≤ 60 gives x = 20, before fabric would allow 40. On the y-axis fabric binds first: 2y ≤ 40 gives y = 20, before stuffing would allow 30.

questions.stem: Students make x koalas and y wombats from leftover materials. A koala uses 1 m of fabric and 3 kg of stuffing; a wombat uses 2 m of fabric and 2 kg of stuffing. They have 40 m of fabric and 60 kg of stuffing. The constraints are x + 2y ≤ 40, 3x + 2y ≤ 60, x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0. The profit is P = 5x + 4y dollars. What is the maximum profit?
questions.explanation: Evaluate P at each vertex: (0, 0) gives $0, (20, 0) gives $100, (10, 15) gives $110 and (0, 20) gives $80. The maximum is $110, making 10 koalas and 15 wombats. $200 uses the point (40, 0), which is not feasible.

questions.stem: Students make x koalas and y wombats from leftover materials. A koala uses 1 m of fabric and 3 kg of stuffing; a wombat uses 2 m of fabric and 2 kg of stuffing. They have 40 m of fabric and 60 kg of stuffing. The constraints are x + 2y ≤ 40, 3x + 2y ≤ 60, x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0. The profit changes to P = 6x + 2y. How much fabric is left over (the wastage) at the new optimal solution?
options: 0 m
5 m
questions.explanation: Now (20, 0) gives $120 against $90 at (10, 15) and $40 at (0, 20), so 20 koalas are made. They use all 60 kg of stuffing but only 20 m of fabric, wasting 20 m. There is no wastage at (10, 15), but that is no longer optimal.

questions.stem: Students make x koalas and y wombats from leftover materials. A koala uses 1 m of fabric and 3 kg of stuffing; a wombat uses 2 m of fabric and 2 kg of stuffing. They have 40 m of fabric and 60 kg of stuffing. The constraints are x + 2y ≤ 40, 3x + 2y ≤ 60, x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0. With profit P = 3x + 2y, the vertices (20, 0) and (10, 15) both give $60. What does this mean?
options: Only the two vertices themselves give the best profit
The problem has no optimal solution at all
The midpoint (15, 7.5) is the single optimal point
Every point on the boundary between them is optimal
questions.explanation: P = 3x + 2y is parallel to the stuffing line 3x + 2y = 60, so the profit is $60 all along that edge. There are multiple optimal solutions, and other factors, such as whole numbers of toys or customer demand, decide between them.

questions.stem: Students make x koalas and y wombats from leftover materials. A koala uses 1 m of fabric and 3 kg of stuffing; a wombat uses 2 m of fabric and 2 kg of stuffing. They have 40 m of fabric and 60 kg of stuffing. The constraints are x + 2y ≤ 40, 3x + 2y ≤ 60, x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0. The profit is P = 5x + 4y. If the stuffing available increases to 72 kg, what is the new maximum profit?
questions.explanation: The stuffing line becomes 3x + 2y = 72, meeting x + 2y = 40 at (16, 12), with axis vertex (24, 0). P is $120 at (24, 0) and $128 at (16, 12), so the maximum rises from $110 to $128. (12, 16) swaps the coordinates.

questions.stem: Students make x koalas and y wombats from leftover materials. A koala uses 1 m of fabric and 3 kg of stuffing; a wombat uses 2 m of fabric and 2 kg of stuffing. They have 40 m of fabric and 60 kg of stuffing. The constraints are x + 2y ≤ 40, 3x + 2y ≤ 60, x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0. Is making 12 koalas and 10 wombats feasible?
options: Yes, it uses 22 m of fabric and 46 kg of stuffing
Yes, it uses 32 m of fabric and 56 kg of stuffing
No, it uses 32 m of fabric and 66 kg of stuffing
No, it uses 34 m of fabric and 56 kg of stuffing
questions.explanation: Fabric is 12 + 2 × 10 = 32 m (at most 40) and stuffing is 3 × 12 + 2 × 10 = 56 kg (at most 60), so both constraints hold and the point is feasible. It is inside the region, not on a boundary, so some of each material is left over.

questions.stem: Students make x koalas and y wombats from leftover materials. A koala uses 1 m of fabric and 3 kg of stuffing; a wombat uses 2 m of fabric and 2 kg of stuffing. They have 40 m of fabric and 60 kg of stuffing. The constraints are x + 2y ≤ 40, 3x + 2y ≤ 60, x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0. At the optimal solution of 10 koalas and 15 wombats, how much of each material is left over?
options: None of either material
10 m of fabric and none of the stuffing
None of the fabric and 15 kg of stuffing
10 m of fabric and 15 kg of stuffing
questions.explanation: Fabric used is 10 + 2 × 15 = 40 m and stuffing used is 3 × 10 + 2 × 15 = 60 kg, so both are used up exactly. The optimum lies where both constraint lines meet, which is why there is no wastage.

questions.stem: A workshop makes x jackets and y vests each day, with x + y ≤ 10 and 5x + 2y ≤ 34 (metres of cloth), x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0. Profit is P = 30x + 20y dollars. The constraint lines meet at a vertex. What are its coordinates, to two decimal places?
questions.explanation: Substituting y = 10 − x into 5x + 2y = 34 gives 3x + 20 = 34, so x = 14/3 ≈ 4.67 and y = 16/3 ≈ 5.33. (4, 6) is a nearby whole-number point, not the vertex itself.

questions.stem: A workshop makes x jackets and y vests each day, with x + y ≤ 10 and 5x + 2y ≤ 34 (metres of cloth), x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0. Profit is P = 30x + 20y dollars. The best vertex is (4.67, 5.33), but only whole garments can be made. What is the best achievable whole-number production?
options: 5 jackets and 5 vests
5 jackets and 6 vests
4 jackets and 5 vests
4 jackets and 6 vests
questions.explanation: Test the whole-number points around the vertex that stay feasible. (5, 5) needs 35 m of cloth, over 34, and (5, 6) breaks both constraints. (4, 6) is feasible with profit $240, beating (4, 5) at $220 and (5, 4) at $230.

questions.stem: Only whole numbers of items can be made, but the optimal vertex is not a whole-number point. What should be done?
options: Round both coordinates of the vertex to the nearest whole number
Round both coordinates of the vertex up to the next whole number
Choose the nearest vertex of the region that lies on an axis
Test nearby whole-number points that lie in the feasible region
questions.explanation: Rounding can push a point outside the feasible region, as rounding up uses more resources than exist. Instead, check the discrete points surrounding the optimum, keep only feasible ones, and compare their objective values.

questions.stem: A workshop makes x jackets and y vests each day, with x + y ≤ 10 and 5x + 2y ≤ 34 (metres of cloth), x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0. Profit is P = 30x + 20y dollars. Why is rounding the vertex (4.67, 5.33) to (5, 5) not acceptable?
options: (5, 5) lies inside the region, so it cannot be optimal
(5, 5) needs 35 m of cloth, but only 34 m is available
(5, 5) needs 11 hours of labour, but only 10 are available
(5, 5) gives less profit than the vertex at (0, 10)
questions.explanation: 5 × 5 + 2 × 5 = 35 m of cloth exceeds the 34 m limit, so (5, 5) is not feasible. It does meet x + y ≤ 10 exactly, and its profit of $250 would be higher than any feasible point, which is why it is tempting.

questions.stem: A farmer mixes x kg of feed A and y kg of feed B. The mix needs 3x + y ≥ 12 units of protein and x + 2y ≥ 9 units of fibre, with x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0. Feed A costs $4/kg and feed B $3/kg. What is the minimum cost of the mix?
questions.explanation: The vertices are (0, 12), (3, 3) and (9, 0). The cost C = 4x + 3y is $36, $21 and $36 there, so the minimum is $21 with 3 kg of each feed. (0, 0) costs nothing but is not feasible, because it provides no protein or fibre.

questions.stem: A farmer mixes x kg of feed A and y kg of feed B. The mix needs 3x + y ≥ 12 units of protein and x + 2y ≥ 9 units of fibre, with x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0. Feed A costs $4/kg and feed B $3/kg. Why is the feasible region for this problem unbounded?
options: The constraints are all ≤, so smaller amounts always satisfy them
The cost function has no maximum value, so the region has no edge
The two constraint lines are parallel, so they never intersect
The constraints are all ≥, so larger amounts always satisfy them
questions.explanation: Any mix with more feed still meets minimum protein and fibre requirements, so the region extends without limit away from the origin. That is fine for minimising cost, where the optimum is still at a vertex.

questions.stem: Which word in a problem usually signals a constraint written with ≥?
options: no more than
up to
at least
at most
questions.explanation: 'At least 12 units' means 12 or more, written ≥ 12. 'At most', 'no more than' and 'up to' all set an upper limit and are written with ≤.

questions.stem: A bakery must make at least twice as many loaves (x) as cakes (y). Which inequality expresses this?
options: y ≥ 2x
2x ≥ y
x + y ≥ 2
x ≥ 2y
questions.explanation: Twice the number of cakes is 2y, and loaves must be at least that, so x ≥ 2y. Writing y ≥ 2x reverses the relationship, a common slip when translating words into symbols.

questions.stem: A cafe sells x pies at $6 profit each and y sausage rolls at $2.50 profit each. Which objective function gives the total profit?
questions.explanation: Each pie adds $6 and each sausage roll adds $2.50, so P = 6x + 2.5y. P = 8.5(x + y) would give each item the combined profit of both.

questions.stem: Which point satisfies all of x + y ≤ 8, 2x + y ≤ 12, x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0?
questions.explanation: (3, 4) gives 7 ≤ 8 and 10 ≤ 12, so it is feasible. (5, 3) gives 13 for 2x + y, (2, 7) gives 9 for x + y, and (7, 0) gives 14 for 2x + y, so each breaks a constraint.

questions.stem: The feasible region x + y ≤ 8, 2x + y ≤ 12, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 has vertices (0, 0), (6, 0), (4, 4) and (0, 8). Where is P = 3x + 5y greatest?
options: (4, 4), where P = 40
(0, 8), where P = 40
(4, 4), where P = 32
(6, 0), where P = 18
questions.explanation: P is 0 at (0, 0), 18 at (6, 0), 32 at (4, 4) and 40 at (0, 8). The intersection of the two constraint lines is often but not always the optimum; here y earns more, so the vertex with the most y wins.

questions.stem: What is the correct order of steps in solving a linear programming problem?
options: Objective function, evaluate, constraints, vertices, compare
Vertices, constraints, evaluate, objective function, compare
Constraints, vertices, compare, objective function, evaluate
Constraints, objective function, vertices, evaluate, compare
questions.explanation: Formulate and graph the constraints, formulate the objective function, identify the feasible region and its vertices, evaluate the objective function at each vertex, then compare the values. Vertices cannot be found before the constraints are graphed.

questions.stem: In linear programming, what does wastage mean?
options: The amount of a resource left unused at the optimal solution
The profit lost by choosing a point inside the region
The difference between the largest and smallest profits
The points that lie outside the feasible region
questions.explanation: Wastage is what remains of an available resource after the optimal plan is carried out. A constraint that passes through the optimal vertex is used up exactly and has no wastage.

questions.stem: In a linear programming problem the profit per item of one product increases. What happens to the objective function line?
options: The constraints change, so new vertices must be calculated
Its slope changes, so a different vertex may become optimal
It moves parallel to itself, so the same vertex stays optimal
The feasible region grows, so every vertex becomes optimal
questions.explanation: Changing a coefficient in P = ax + by changes the slope of the profit lines, so the last vertex they touch may change. The constraints, and so the feasible region and its vertices, stay the same.

questions.stem: In a linear programming problem one resource becomes more plentiful. What changes?
options: Nothing changes, because the objective function is the same
The non-negativity constraints change to allow negative values
That constraint line moves, so the region and vertices change
The objective function changes slope, but the region stays fixed
questions.explanation: More of a resource moves its constraint line further from the origin, enlarging the feasible region and shifting its vertices, so the optimal solution and wastage may change. The objective function only changes if profits or costs change.

questions.stem: In which situation is it acceptable to give a non-whole-number optimal solution such as x = 4.6?
options: x is kilograms of a feed mixed for stock
x is the number of buses booked for a trip
x is the number of jackets sewn in a day
x is the number of staff rostered for a shift
questions.explanation: Kilograms of feed are a continuous quantity, so 4.6 kg makes sense. Buses, jackets and staff are discrete, so the solution must be adjusted to a feasible whole-number point.

questions.stem: Two vertices of a feasible region give the same maximum profit. Besides profit, which consideration could sensibly decide between them?
options: Which option has the larger x-coordinate by default
Which option is closer to the origin on the graph
Which option lies on the first constraint graphed
Which option leaves less of each resource unused
questions.explanation: When there are multiple optimal solutions, students consider factors beyond the objective value, such as wastage, demand or storage. The size of a coordinate or the order constraints were graphed has no meaning in the context.

questions.stem: Students make x koalas and y wombats from leftover materials. A koala uses 1 m of fabric and 3 kg of stuffing; a wombat uses 2 m of fabric and 2 kg of stuffing. They have 40 m of fabric and 60 kg of stuffing. The constraints are x + 2y ≤ 40, 3x + 2y ≤ 60, x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0. A trial-and-error student tries 20 koalas and 0 wombats, then 0 koalas and 20 wombats. What does the graphical method show that this misses?
options: Making only koalas always gives the greatest possible profit
Making only wombats always gives the greatest possible profit
The best mix is always an equal number of each toy
Combining both toys at (10, 15) gives more profit than either
questions.explanation: With P = 5x + 4y, (20, 0) gives $100 and (0, 20) gives $80, but the vertex (10, 15) where both materials run out gives $110. An equal split such as (12, 12) is feasible but earns only $108.

questions.stem: What is a vertex of a feasible region?
options: The point where the objective function equals zero
The midpoint of one edge of the feasible region
A corner point where two boundary lines meet
Any point that lies inside the feasible region
questions.explanation: The vertices are the corner points of the region, found by solving pairs of boundary equations simultaneously. They are the only points that need testing in the objective function.

questions.stem: Students make x koalas and y wombats from leftover materials. A koala uses 1 m of fabric and 3 kg of stuffing; a wombat uses 2 m of fabric and 2 kg of stuffing. They have 40 m of fabric and 60 kg of stuffing. What does the boundary line x + 2y = 40 represent?
options: Combinations of toys that use all the fabric exactly
Combinations of toys that use all the stuffing exactly
Combinations of toys that give the greatest profit
Combinations of toys that use no fabric at all
questions.explanation: Points on x + 2y = 40 use exactly 40 m of fabric; points below it use less. Combinations that use all the stuffing lie on 3x + 2y = 60.

questions.stem: A farmer mixes x kg of feed A and y kg of feed B. The mix needs 3x + y ≥ 12 units of protein and x + 2y ≥ 9 units of fibre, with x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0. Feed A costs $4/kg and feed B $3/kg. If the farmer uses only feed B, the cheapest such mix is (0, 12). How many units of fibre does it supply beyond the minimum?
questions.explanation: At (0, 12) the fibre supplied is 0 + 2 × 12 = 24 units, which is 15 more than the 9 required. Protein is exactly 12, so that constraint is the one binding at this vertex. 24 is the total fibre, not the excess.

questions.stem: Why is the graphical method preferred to trial and error for linear programming?
options: It always gives a whole-number answer for each variable
It avoids the need to write down any of the constraints
It shows that the optimum always uses equal amounts
Only the vertices need testing, so the optimum is certain
questions.explanation: Trial and error may miss the best combination, while the graph shows every feasible point and the optimum must lie at a vertex. The method still needs the constraints, and its answer may not be a whole number.
